name: Nathu La
tagline: The India–China border pass at 4,310 m, open to Indians Wed–Sun
meta_description: Nathu La pass at 4,310 m: permits for Indian nationals, Wed–Sun opening, 1967 clashes, Sherathang trade mart, costs from Gangtok, indicative 2026.
summary: Nathu La is a 4,310 m pass on the India–China border, about 56 km and 3 hours from Gangtok via Tsomgo Lake. Only Indian nationals may visit, on a Protected Area Permit through a registered agent, usually Wednesday to Sunday. It was the old Gangtok–Lhasa trade route and saw clashes in 1967. Check current status before you travel.
intro: Nathu La is where the old mule road from Gangtok crossed into Tibet, and where Indian and Chinese soldiers now stand closer to each other than almost anywhere else on the border. The pass sits at 4,310 m on the Dongkya Range, about 18 km by road beyond Tsomgo Lake. On a clear morning you look down into the Chumbi Valley of Tibet. On most afternoons you look into cloud and feel the wind, which rarely stops up here.

A visit is short and controlled. Cars park below the pass, and the Army guides visitors up a flight of steps to a viewing area by the fence. You will be told where you can and cannot take photographs, and how long you may stay. Most groups spend 20 to 40 minutes at the top. That is the right length, because at this height the steps alone leave many people short of breath and a little dizzy.

Nathu La is for Indian nationals only. Foreign nationals, including OCI card holders, are not issued permits. The pass is generally open to tourists Wednesday to Sunday and shut on Monday and Tuesday, and it closes at short notice after heavy snow. We pair it with Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir on one long day from Gangtok, and we always keep a spare day in the plan in case the pass is shut on the morning you go. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: A trade road, a war line and a reopening
paras: In 1873 J. W. Edgar, the Deputy Commissioner of Darjeeling, surveyed the passes into Tibet and found Tibetan traders using Nathu La. Francis Younghusband's expedition crossed it in 1903–04. In the 1950s it carried much of the trade between India and Tibet: before 1962, mule trains of about 200 animals, each loaded with about 80 kg, took 20 to 25 days from Gangtok to Lhasa. Cloth, grain, soap and even dismantled cars went north. Wool, silk, musk and medicinal herbs came south.

The 1962 war closed the pass. In September 1967 Indian and Chinese troops fought at Nathu La, and again at nearby Cho La that October, with deaths on both sides. The pass stayed shut for more than four decades. On 6 July 2006 it reopened for border trade, with a trade mart at Sherathang on the Indian side, and in 2015 it opened as a route for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage. Trade was halted again in 2020, and in August 2025 India and China agreed to reopen it; check current status before you travel.
story.source: Wikipedia articles Nathu La, Nathu La and Cho La clashes, and Sherathang; J. W. Edgar's 1874 report

did_you_know: The Gangtok–Nathu La road was made motorable between 1954 and 1958 and formally opened by Jawaharlal Nehru on 17 September 1958; at the time it ended at Sherathang.
The 14th Dalai Lama travelled to India over Nathu La in the autumn of 1956 for the 2,500th birth anniversary of the Buddha.
Nathu La is one of the official Border Personnel Meeting points where Indian and Chinese Army officers meet on set occasions.
facts: India–China border, 1967 clashes, old Tibet trade route

highlights.title: The border viewing area at 4,310 m
highlights.text: Army staff lead visitors up steps to a viewing area beside the fence, where the road into Tibet's Chumbi Valley drops away. Chinese posts are in plain view. Follow every instruction, keep the visit short, and photograph only where you are told you may.

highlights.title: The old road over the Dongkya Range
highlights.text: The road from Tsomgo climbs another 550 m in about 18 km, past Army camps and bare slopes where yaks graze. In clear weather you see ridge after ridge of the Dongkya Range. In winter the snow banks along the road can be taller than the car.

highlights.title: Sherathang trade mart
highlights.text: Just below the pass is Sherathang, the Indian trade mart agreed with China in 2003 and opened in 2006. Its sheds and customs post mark the revived trade route. Trade has been halted since 2020, so treat it as a sight from the road. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: The 1967 war memorial
highlights.text: The war memorial at Sherathang honours Indian soldiers killed in the Nathu La and Cho La clashes of September and October 1967. It is a quiet, well-kept place. If your driver stops, take two minutes to read the names and the account of the fighting.

highlights.title: Tsomgo and Baba Mandir on the same day
highlights.text: The usual day plan is Gangtok to Tsomgo Lake, up to Nathu La, then Baba Mandir on the way down. It takes 8 to 9 hours, back by late afternoon. A reserved car for all three costs ₹6,500–9,000, indicative 2026.

how_to_reach.text: Some Gangtok agents sell shared seats on the Tsomgo–Baba Mandir–Nathu La day, usually ₹1,000–1,800 a person including permit handling, indicative 2026. Seats fill fastest Friday to Sunday. Submit photos and ID a day or two ahead. Check current status before you travel.

A Gangtok-registered Bolero, Scorpio or Xylo for Tsomgo, Nathu La and Baba Mandir costs ₹6,500–9,000 per vehicle for up to five people, indicative 2026. The agent files the permit with your documents. Cars from outside Sikkim are not allowed. Check current status before you travel.

Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive about 125 km to Gangtok. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights as of 2026. Sleep at least one night in Gangtok before going to Nathu La to give your body time to adjust.

where_to_stay: There is nowhere for tourists to stay at Nathu La; it is a day visit, and you sleep in Gangtok, 56 km below. We suggest two nights in Gangtok before the trip, so you are not climbing to 4,310 m straight off the plains. On a budget, Hotel Sonam Delek and Hotel Tibet are close to MG Marg for the early pick-up. Netuk House on Tibet Road is a comfortable mid-range heritage stay. Elgin Nor-Khill and Taj Guras Kutir suit a higher budget. Ask your hotel to file the permit; most work with registered agents every day.
costs: Reserved car, Tsomgo + Nathu La + Baba Mandir
Shared seat, Nathu La day tour
Tea and snacks on the way
budget_tip: Book the Nathu La car for a Wednesday or Thursday rather than a weekend: permits are easier to get, shared seats are more often available, and the queue at the steps is shorter.
tips: Only Indian nationals can visit Nathu La; carry the original photo ID you gave for the permit, because it is checked against the list.
Operators usually will not take children under 5 to Nathu La, and we advise against taking infants to 4,310 m at all.
Climb the steps at the pass slowly, stop when you need to, and spend no more than 30–40 minutes at the top.
Wear layers, a windproof jacket, gloves and a cap even in May; the wind at the pass makes it feel well below freezing.
If snow is forecast, ask your agent the evening before whether Nathu La permits are being issued, and keep Tsomgo as a fallback.

experiences.title: A short visit to the border at 4,310 m
experiences.best_time: Arrive by 11 am, Wed–Sun, Apr–May and Oct–Nov
experiences.cost: Included in the Nathu La car; permit ≈ ₹200
experiences.summary: The pass itself: a flight of steps from the car park to a viewing area by the India–China fence, with Army staff setting the rules. Short, cold and windy, and for many people the highest point they will ever stand on.
body: Cars stop at a parking area below the pass. From there you walk up a flight of steps to the viewing area by the border fence. The climb is short, but at 4,310 m it feels long. Go one step at a time and stop when you need to. At the top, Army staff will tell you where to stand, what you may photograph and how long you can stay. Follow them exactly.

On a clear day you look east into the Chumbi Valley of Tibet, with Chinese buildings and soldiers in plain view across the fence. The pass is one of the places where the two armies are closest along the whole border. Do not shout, gesture or try to talk across the line, and never point a camera where a sign or a soldier says no. This is a working frontier, not a theme park.

Most groups spend 20 to 40 minutes at the top. Weather turns quickly: wind, cloud and snow can arrive within an hour, and temperatures in winter fall far below freezing. If anyone in your group feels a pounding headache, nausea or confusion, head down at once. Getting lower is the only real cure. Save the photos for the walk back to the car, and keep a flask of warm water in the vehicle for the ride down.

faqs.q: How many steps are there at Nathu La
faqs.a: There is a flight of steps from the parking area up to the border viewing area; counts given by visitors vary, and it takes most people 10 to 15 minutes at a slow pace. The steps are not steep, but at 4,310 m every one feels heavy. Stop when you need to, let others pass, and do not race. Seniors can wait in the car if they feel unwell.

faqs.q: Can we take photos at Nathu La
faqs.a: Yes, in the places the Army allows. Some spots, including parts of the fence and any military structures, are off limits for cameras, and staff will tell you. Ignoring them can mean your phone is checked or the group is sent down. Keep drones at home; they are not allowed. When in doubt, ask the soldier on duty before you lift the camera.

faqs.q: Can you see Chinese soldiers at Nathu La
faqs.a: Often, yes. The posts on both sides are very close, and Chinese buildings and soldiers are usually visible across the fence. Behave as you would at any international border: no shouting, gestures or attempts to talk across the line, and no photos where they are forbidden. The Army may limit numbers or close the area at short notice.

experiences.title: Sherathang war memorial and the 1967 clashes
experiences.best_time: On the way to or from the pass
experiences.wiki: Nathu La and Cho La clashes
experiences.summary: A small, well-kept memorial at Sherathang, just below the pass, for Indian soldiers killed in the Nathu La and Cho La clashes of 1967. Read the names and the short account, and you will see the border differently on the way up.
body: After the 1962 war, Nathu La stayed tense. Both armies dug in along the crest, and arguments over where exactly the line ran grew sharper. Fighting broke out on 11 September 1967, when Chinese forces attacked Indian posts at the pass, and lasted until 15 September, with artillery fire on both sides. In October 1967 another clash took place at Cho La, a pass to the north. Both sides lost men, and the accounts of numbers still differ.

Independent accounts describe a decisive tactical advantage for the Indian Army, which held its positions. The memorial at Sherathang honours the Indian soldiers who died in both clashes. It is a short stop, and drivers include it when time and Army rules allow. Ask in the morning rather than on the way down, when everyone is tired, the light is going and the cloud is closing in over the road.

Treat it as you would any war grave. Remove caps if asked, keep voices low and do not climb on the structures. Photographs are usually allowed, but check with any soldier present. For many Indian visitors, this is the part of the day that stays with them longest, more than the pass itself. Take a moment, read the plaques, and remember that young men served here in the cold, far from home, as soldiers still do today.

faqs.q: What happened at Nathu La in 1967
faqs.a: Between 11 and 15 September 1967, Indian and Chinese troops fought at Nathu La after a dispute over the border fence turned into an attack on Indian posts, followed by artillery fire. A second clash took place at Cho La in October 1967. There were deaths on both sides, and the Indian Army held its positions. The Sherathang memorial honours the Indian soldiers who died.

faqs.q: Where is the Nathu La war memorial
faqs.a: The war memorial for the 1967 Nathu La and Cho La clashes stands at Sherathang, a few kilometres below the pass on the Indian side, close to the trade mart. Drivers usually stop there on the way up or down if time and Army rules allow. There is no separate ticket. Ask your driver in the morning so he can plan the stop.

faqs.q: Is Sherathang open to foreigners
faqs.a: No. Sherathang lies beyond Tsomgo Lake on the Nathu La road, and foreign nationals are not given permits past the lake. The memorial, trade mart and pass are for Indian nationals on a Protected Area Permit arranged through a registered agent. Foreign visitors can still see Tsomgo Lake on a day permit. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sherathang trade mart and the wool road
experiences.summary: Sherathang is the Indian trade mart for the India–China border trade through Nathu La, agreed in 2003 and opened in 2006. A short look at it, and the story of the mule trains before 1962, explains why this pass mattered.
body: For centuries, goods moved over these passes on mules and yaks. Traders called it the wool road more than the silk road: Tibetan wool came south to Kalimpong and Gangtok, and cloth, grain, kerosene and tools went north. Before 1962, about 200 mules worked the Gangtok–Lhasa run, each carrying about 80 kg, and the trip took 20 to 25 days. Most of it ran through about 200 licensed trading firms.

In 2003 India and China agreed on Sherathang, on the Indian side, and Rinqingang, on the Tibetan side, as border trade marts. Trade reopened on 6 July 2006, limited to a list of goods and a few days a week in the warmer months. It never reached the early forecasts, partly because of narrow roads and short seasons. Trade was halted in 2020 during the pandemic and border tensions; in August 2025 the two governments agreed to reopen it. Check current status before you travel.

Sherathang also has a mail exchange point: letters between India Post and China Post have been handed over here on set days. For a visitor, there is little to buy. The value of the stop is seeing a working frontier town at about 4,100 m, the sheds where trucks are checked, and the road beyond it that once carried mule bells all the way to Lhasa. Ten minutes here makes the whole Silk Route story easier to picture.

faqs.q: Can tourists shop at the Nathu La trade mart
faqs.a: Not really. Sherathang is a border trade mart for licensed traders from Sikkim and Tibet, not a tourist market, and trade has been halted since 2020. You can see it from the road and stop briefly if the driver and Army allow. For shopping, Lal Bazaar and MG Marg in Gangtok are better bets. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When did Nathu La reopen for trade
faqs.a: Nathu La reopened for India–China border trade on 6 July 2006, after being sealed since the 1962 war. The 2003 agreement named Sherathang in India and Rinqingang in Tibet as the trade marts. Trade ran on set weekdays in the warmer months until it was halted in 2020. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is it called the Silk Route
faqs.a: Mostly as a modern label. Silk did cross these passes, but the main trade was wool from Tibet, carried on mules to Kalimpong and Gangtok, with cloth, grain and manufactured goods going back. Traders who worked the route have called it the wool road. Today Silk Route usually means the Zuluk–Nathang–Kupup road, which joins the Nathu La road near Baba Mandir.

experiences.title: The Tsomgo, Nathu La and Baba Mandir day
experiences.best_time: Wed–Sun, Apr–May and Oct–Nov; leave by 7 am
experiences.image_query: Tsomgo Lake Nathu La road Sikkim
experiences.summary: The classic day from Gangtok: Tsomgo Lake, the climb to Nathu La, and Baba Mandir on the way down. It covers about 110–120 km and three high stops, so pace it well and start early to beat the afternoon cloud.
body: Leave Gangtok at 7 am. The road climbs past the permit check post to Tsomgo Lake in about 2 hours. Many drivers continue straight to Nathu La first, about 18 km on, because the pass is the stop most likely to cloud over. Arrive by 10 or 11 am, climb the steps slowly and spend 30 to 40 minutes at the top. Sherathang and its war memorial are just below.

On the way down, the road drops to Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir, the Army shrine to a soldier who died in 1968, where you can take tea and see his room and belongings. Then you return to Tsomgo for a short walk or yak ride on the shore. This order puts the highest stop in the morning and the lowest last, which is easier on the body as the day goes on.

Expect to be back in Gangtok by 4 or 5 pm. A reserved car costs ₹6,500–9,000 for up to five people, indicative 2026, and shared seats run ₹1,000–1,800 a head. Pack water, dry snacks, sunscreen, a cap and gloves. If the agent says Nathu La is shut that day, the car usually does Tsomgo and Baba Mandir at a lower rate, and the difference should come back to you. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we do Tsomgo, Nathu La and Baba Mandir in one day
faqs.a: Yes, that is the usual plan. Leave Gangtok by 7 am, go to Tsomgo and then straight up to Nathu La, visit Baba Mandir on the way down and stop at the lake again on the return. It takes 8 to 9 hours. Nathu La is open to tourists Wednesday to Sunday. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What if Nathu La is closed on our date
faqs.a: It happens, mostly after snowfall or for Army reasons, and on Monday and Tuesday by routine. The agent will usually offer Tsomgo and Baba Mandir instead, at the lower rate of about ₹4,500–6,500 per car, indicative 2026. Keep one spare day in Gangtok so you can try again. Ask the evening before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Nathu La day trip tiring
faqs.a: Yes, for most people. You climb from 1,650 m to 4,310 m in about three hours, spend the day above 3,700 m and sit in the car for six or seven hours on winding roads. Sleep well the night before, eat a light breakfast, drink water steadily and avoid alcohol. Seniors and children often enjoy it more if you skip Nathu La and keep it to Tsomgo.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Nathu La
faqs.a: No. Nathu La is open only to Indian nationals. Foreign nationals, including OCI card holders, are not issued permits for the pass, and they are generally not allowed beyond Tsomgo Lake on this road. Foreigners can still visit Tsomgo on a day permit arranged by a registered agent, usually in a group of two or more. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which days is Nathu La open for tourists
faqs.a: Nathu La is generally open to tourists from Wednesday to Sunday and closed on Monday and Tuesday. It also shuts at short notice after heavy snow, during Army activity or on special occasions. Permits are filed a day or more in advance, so plan your Gangtok days with that in mind. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get a Nathu La permit
faqs.a: Through a registered Gangtok travel agent, or your hotel, which works with one. Give them two passport-size photos and a copy of an Indian photo ID per person, a day or two ahead. The Protected Area Permit costs about ₹200 a person through an agent and is issued with the vehicle permit. Carry the original ID. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are children allowed at Nathu La
faqs.a: Operators usually will not take children under 5 to Nathu La, and many hotels and agents will say so when you book. Even for older children, 4,310 m is a big height to reach in three hours. Keep them warm, watch for headache, vomiting or drowsiness, and go down at once if they appear. Tsomgo alone is a gentler day for young families.

faqs.q: How high is Nathu La and will I get altitude sickness
faqs.a: Nathu La is at 4,310 m, more than 2,600 m above Gangtok. Headache, breathlessness and tiredness are common, and a few people get proper acute mountain sickness. Spend a night or two in Gangtok first, climb the steps slowly, stay 30–40 minutes and descend if you feel worse. People with heart or lung conditions, or who are pregnant, should consult a doctor.

faqs.q: How much does a Nathu La trip cost from Gangtok
faqs.a: A reserved car for Tsomgo, Nathu La and Baba Mandir costs about ₹6,500–9,000 per vehicle for up to five people. Shared seats run about ₹1,000–1,800 a person. Add the permit at about ₹200 a person, and ₹100–300 for coat and boot hire in winter. All figures are indicative, 2026.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Nathu La
faqs.a: April–May and October–November are the most reliable. Spring brings melting snow and flowers lower down, and autumn has the clearest skies. December to March means deep snow and frequent closures, though it is spectacular when open. June to September is wet and cloudy, with landslide risk on the roads to Gangtok. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nathu La closed in winter
faqs.a: Not for the whole winter, but often. Between December and March the road beyond Tsomgo is frequently closed for a day or more after heavy snow, until it is cleared. Many winter visitors reach only Tsomgo or Baba Mandir. If seeing the pass matters, plan two or three spare days in Gangtok. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see the Kailash Mansarovar route at Nathu La
faqs.a: The pass you stand at is the route. Since 2015 one of the official Kailash Mansarovar Yatra routes has crossed Nathu La into Tibet, for pilgrims selected through the Government of India's process. Tourists cannot cross; they stay on the Indian side. The yatra has been suspended in some years, so check current status before you travel.
